Content:
We can combine vertical and horizontal shifts and stretches to get new transformed sine and cosine curves. For example, let's draw the graph of the curve
[MATH: y = 2 \cos\left(x+ 2\right) - 1.]

Content:
To plot the given curve, we follow these steps:

Content:
- Start with the graph of [MATH: y=\cos{x}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ada7f7603853d35bcf0e03ac54d53157]

Content:
- Then, stretch it parallel to the [MATH: y]-axis by a stretch factor of [MATH: 2] to give [MATH: y=2\cos{x}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1b0c78d79016771cccd6aa50fb60bf02]

Content:
- Next, shift to the left by [MATH: 2] units to give [MATH: y=2\cos(x + 2).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/504ee16c673208beb2774641c5e66863]

Content:
- Finally, shift it down by [MATH: 1] unit to give [MATH: y=2\cos\left(x + 2\right) - 1.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/02789c684c86be83fdb2c38704233384]

sections.normalized_html: The graph above shows the function [MATH: y=2\sin{(x+C)},] where [MATH: C] is a constant. Given that [MATH: -\pi < C < \pi,] what is the value of [MATH: C?]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/18432f4bbf6c1b1d25ed7b28e8a18a15]

The graph above shows the function [MATH: y=2\sin{(x+C)},] where [MATH: C] is a constant. Given that [MATH: -\pi < C < \pi,] what is the value of [MATH: C?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The constant [MATH: C] is the phase shift of the function.

To plot the given function, we follow these steps:

  • Take the graph of [MATH: y=\sin x.]

  • Vertically stretch it by a scale factor of [MATH: 2] to give [MATH: y = 2 \sin x.]

  • Then, shift it by [MATH: 2] units right to give [MATH: y=2\sin \left(x-2\right).]

Therefore, [MATH: C=-2.]

items.title: Identifying the Vertical Stretch of a Transformed Sine or Cosine Curve

sections.normalized_html: The graph above shows the function [MATH: y=A\cos\left(x+2\right),] where [MATH: A] is a constant. What is [MATH: A?]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/5e0c2c562d9337497b4b8c194e38cd14]

The graph above shows the function [MATH: y=A\cos\left(x+2\right),] where [MATH: A] is a constant. What is [MATH: A?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The constant [MATH: A] is the amplitude of the function.

From the graph, we see that the maximum value is [MATH: y_\max=\sqrt{2}] and the minimum value is [MATH: y_\min=-\sqrt{2}.] Therefore, the amplitude is [MATH: A = \dfrac{y_\max-y_\min}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}-(-\sqrt{2})}{2}=\sqrt{2}.]

items.title: Identifying the Horizontal Stretch of a Transformed Sine or Cosine Curve

sections.normalized_html: The graph above shows the function [MATH: y=4\sin{(Bx)},] where [MATH: B] is a positive constant. What is [MATH: B?]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/8f5530a7155089ee92031b433f06893f]

The graph above shows the function [MATH: y=4\sin{(Bx)},] where [MATH: B] is a positive constant. What is [MATH: B?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The constant [MATH: B] is the horizontal stretch of the function.

We can see that the function repeats itself [MATH: 3] times in the interval [MATH: x\in[0,2\pi].] Therefore, the period [MATH: T] of the function is

[MATH: T = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}.]

The formula for the period [MATH: T] of the function [MATH: y=A\sin(Bx + C) + D] is given by

[MATH: T = \dfrac{2\pi}{B}.]

Applying the formula for the period, we get

[MATH: \dfrac{2\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{B}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad B = \dfrac{2\pi}{\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)} = 3.]

Therefore, [MATH: B=3.]
